profile.tagline: Grandma's Pampanga recipes, served sizzling.
profile.story: Lola Pacing began cooking for her neighbors on a single charcoal grill, and the line outside her kitchen grew every weekend. Today her grandchildren run the dining room and keep her recipes exactly as she wrote them, from the crisp-edged sisig to the sour, tamarind-rich sinigang.
profile.funFact: The sisig plate arrives so hot that the sizzle can still be heard at the next table.
profile.reservations: Recommended for groups of six or more

profile.tagline: Classic Filipino flavors with a modern twist.
profile.story: Named after the traditional nipa hut, this bistro pairs old family dishes with new techniques. Chefs smoke the adobo, plate the kare-kare like a painting and serve halo-halo with house-made ube ice cream.
profile.funFact: The bamboo ceiling is built from a real nipa hut frame saved from a demolished house.
profile.reservations: Recommended on weekends

profile.tagline: Eight seats, one chef, and the season on a plate.
profile.story: The chef trained for twelve years before opening this eight-seat counter. The menu changes with the market, and each piece of sushi is handed to you the moment it is ready, so you can eat it at its best.
profile.funFact: Guests are asked to arrive on time so every piece is served at the same moment.
profile.reservations: Required, booked at least one week ahead
dietaryOptions: please tell us about allergies when booking

profile.tagline: A red lantern, a steaming bowl and a very short wait.
profile.story: Hidden down a narrow lane, Ichiban Noodle Lantern is known for its pork and chicken broth, simmered for fourteen hours. Diners order from a ticket machine, take a seat at the counter and are slurping within minutes.
profile.funFact: The red lantern outside has hung in the same spot since the day the shop opened.
profile.reservations: Not accepted

profile.tagline: Rome on a plate, the way Nonna Rosa made it.
profile.story: In a small street near Campo de' Fiori, Nonna Rosa's family still rolls pasta by hand each morning. The carbonara follows the traditional recipe with egg, pecorino and cured pork cheek, and the tiramisù is made fresh every afternoon.
profile.funFact: The pasta table in the dining room is the same one Nonna Rosa used in her own kitchen.
profile.reservations: Recommended for dinner

profile.tagline: Blistered crust, wood fire, nothing to hide.
profile.story: Forno Azzurro bakes Neapolitan pizza in a wood-fired oven that burns at about 450 degrees Celsius. A pizza cooks in under two minutes, which is why the crust is soft in the middle and blistered at the edge.
profile.funFact: The dough rests for twenty-four hours before it ever meets the oven.
profile.reservations: Not accepted; expect a short wait

profile.tagline: Seven moles, one corn field and a very long table.
profile.story: La Milpa takes its name from the traditional Mexican field where corn, beans and squash grow together. The kitchen grinds its own corn, toasts its own chiles and serves a mole that takes three days to prepare.
profile.funFact: The tortillas are pressed by hand and cooked on a clay comal in the dining room.
profile.reservations: Recommended for dinner

profile.tagline: The lighthouse of late-night tacos.
profile.story: El Faro started as a cart with a single lamp and now has a full counter, but the spinning trompo of marinated pork is still the star. Locals come after midnight for tacos al pastor topped with pineapple, cilantro and onion.
profile.funFact: The trompo is lit every day at noon and has never been late once.
profile.reservations: Not accepted

profile.tagline: A chestnut tree, a chalkboard menu and a proper bistro.
profile.story: A tall chestnut tree shades the terrace of this neighborhood bistro. The chalkboard menu changes daily, the coq au vin has stayed on it for two decades, and the chef personally chooses the cheese at the market each morning.
profile.funFact: The chalkboard is erased and rewritten by hand every morning at nine.
profile.openingHours: Tue to Sun, 12:00 to 14:30 and 19:00 to 22:30
profile.reservations: Recommended

profile.tagline: Golden bread from the first light of morning.
profile.story: The bakers at Maison du Pain Doré start work at two in the morning so the first baguettes are ready by half past six. The shop also makes butter croissants with more than eighty layers and a praline tart that is a Lyon favorite.
profile.funFact: A bell rings each time a fresh tray of baguettes leaves the oven.
profile.reservations: Not needed

profile.tagline: A journey through India, one spice at a time.
profile.story: The menu at Spice Route Kitchen follows the old spice trade routes, with dishes from Kerala, Punjab, Gujarat and Maharashtra. The thali arrives with eleven small bowls, and the cooks grind their spice blends fresh every morning.
profile.funFact: The spice wall at the entrance shows more than sixty spices to smell and touch.
profile.reservations: Recommended on weekends

profile.tagline: Crisp dosas, hot filter coffee, no hurry.
profile.story: Dosa Darbar serves breakfast all day. The dosa batter ferments overnight, the chutneys are ground to order and the filter coffee is poured from a height in the traditional style, creating the perfect froth.
profile.funFact: The largest dosa on the menu is nearly one meter long.
profile.reservations: Not accepted
dietaryOptions: vegan options marked on the menu

profile.tagline: The bowl that made Chiang Mai famous.
profile.story: In a wooden house with a garden, Baan Khao Soi serves the Northern Thai specialties the region is known for. The khao soi curry is simmered with coconut milk and spices, then topped with crispy egg noodles and served with pickled mustard greens and lime.
profile.funFact: Each bowl is served with a small plate of pickled greens, shallots and lime to build your own flavor.
profile.reservations: Recommended for lunch

profile.tagline: Wok flames, night lights and plastic stools.
profile.story: Soi Nine Street Kitchen brings the energy of a Bangkok night market to one open-air kitchen. Cooks work over roaring woks, and the pad Thai arrives with a wedge of lime, crushed peanuts and a sprinkle of chili.
profile.funFact: The wok flame can reach the ceiling lanterns, and diners cheer when it does.
profile.reservations: Not accepted

profile.tagline: Boiled, baked and loaded since sunrise.
profile.story: Five Boroughs Bagel Co. boils its bagels in malt water and bakes them on wooden boards, the old-fashioned New York way. The line at the counter moves fast, and the most popular order is an everything bagel with cream cheese and smoked salmon.
profile.funFact: The owner keeps a map with a pin for every borough a customer has traveled from.
profile.reservations: Not needed
dietaryOptions: Vegan cream cheese and gluten-free bagels available

profile.tagline: Big, thin, foldable and open late.
profile.story: Corner Slice sells large New York-style slices with a crisp base and a bubbly edge. The plain cheese slice is the benchmark, and regulars fold it in half, just like they have done for decades.
profile.funFact: The oven has been lit every day for over thirty years without a single day off.
profile.reservations: Not accepted
